Determine, for each query on a tree (with one extra optional shortcut edge), whether there exists a path between two given nodes whose length does not exceed k and has the required parity (even or odd).

2. Core algorithmic approach  
- Preprocess the tree for lowest common ancestor (LCA) queries using an Euler‐tour + Range‐Minimum‐Query sparse‐table (RangeQuery) approach, giving O(1) LCA and distance computations per query.  
- Use BFS from the root to compute depths for distance formulas.  
- For each query, compute the direct distance and two “detour” distances that use the extra edge, track the minimum even and odd distances, and compare with k.

3. Reusable components  
- RangeQuery: a generic sparse‐table implementation supporting idempotent range queries (min, max, gcd, etc.).  
- LCA class: builds an Euler tour with first‐visit times and wraps the RangeQuery to answer LCA(a,b) in O(1).  
- dist(a,b) pattern: computes distance via depth[a] + depth[b] − 2·depth[LCA(a,b)].

- Early‐termination check: for each ancestor value, only update and compare once its count reaches the target k, allowing a running best answer to prune further work.

4107-434_A. Ryouko's Memory Note

1. One-sentence summary  
Given a sequence of values, compute the total sum of absolute differences between consecutive elements, then determine how much this sum can be reduced by “re-routing” all transitions involving any single value to their median neighbor.

2. Core algorithmic approach  
• Group transitions by value, collecting for each distinct value the list of neighbors it switches to.  
• For each group, sort the neighbor list and use the fact that the median minimizes the sum of absolute deviations (an L₁‐optimality property) to compute the maximum reduction (“profit”) in the total distance if all those transitions were reconnected through the median.  
• Greedily pick the best single-value re-routing to subtract from the original total.

3. Reusable components  
• median(a): Given a list a, returns its median (handling even/odd lengths) in O(n log n) due to the sort call.  
• profit(a, old_val): Computes the reduction in sum of absolute differences achieved by replacing old_val with the median of a.  
• Transition grouping: Building a dictionary mapping each value to its list of neighbors, and tracking the total sum of |difference| over all consecutive pairs.

Given a functional graph defined by a permutation, determine whether its nodes can be connected into a single tree under the constraint that every cycle is either a fixed‐point or of even length, and if so, output one such spanning‐tree edge set.

2. Core algorithmic approach  
• Cycle decomposition by following each unvisited node’s functional edges until returning to the start (O(n) total).  
• Case analysis on the minimum cycle length:  
  – If there is a 1‐cycle, use it as a universal root (star).  
  – Else if all cycles are even, pick one 2‐cycle and alternately attach other cycles to its two nodes.  
  – Otherwise, report impossibility.

3. Reusable components  
• Cycle detection in a functional graph: iterate from each unmarked node, traverse pointers until you return, then backfill cycle length for all involved nodes.  
• Case‐by‐case tree construction from cycle metadata:  
  – Star‐like attachment around a 1‐cycle root.  
  – Alternating-bipartite attachment pattern for even cycles using a 2‐cycle seed.  
• Edge‐list assembly with zero‐based to one‐based index adjustment.
4738-598_F. Cut Length

1. One-sentence summary  
Given a simple closed polygon, for each query directed line segment, the solution computes the total length of the portion of that segment that lies strictly inside the polygon.  

2. Core algorithmic approach  
It uses computational‐geometry event sweeping: for each query it  
- parameterizes the infinite line by t,  
- finds all intersection parameters t_i where the line crosses a polygon edge (tagged as entering or exiting by signed cross‐product),  
- sorts these events by t_i,  
- and then does a 1D sweep over t accumulating intervals where the “inside‐polygon” parity is nonzero.  

3. Reusable components  
- Intersection-parameter computation: Given a query ray (x0,y0)+(t·dx,t·dy) and a segment from (bx,by) to (bx+abx,by+aby), compute t = ((bx−x0)*aby − (by−y0)*abx)/(dx*aby−dy*abx).  
- Crossing‐direction test: Use sign of ( (bx−x0)*dy − (by−y0)*dx ) to label each intersection as an entry (+1) or exit (−1).  
- Event-sweep pattern: Collect (t,±1) events, sort by t, then scan to accumulate total “inside” t-interval length, finally scaling by hypot(dx,dy).

Compute, for each fixed target point, the first time a single point moving at 45° on a rectangular grid with perfect reflections will visit that target.

2. Core algorithmic approach  
Simulate the 45° motion by “unfolding” reflections into a toroidal grid of size (2·width)×(2·height), group all target points by the invariant diagonal (y–x), then sweep along that diagonal in time-increasing order until the moving point completes one full cycle.

- Cycle detection & stepping: advance the current position to the next boundary in O(1) by taking the minimum of the remaining x- and y-distances, and detect completion when both coordinates are simultaneously at original-modulo positions.

   - Inclusion–exclusion implemented by iterating over all 2^M subsets of the M paths, computing the union of their edge-sets via bitmasks, counting set bits (popcount), and adding or subtracting 2^(N−1−|union|) according to subset parity (O(2^M⋅(N+popcnt_cost))).

   - make_tree(graph, root): builds depth and parent arrays on a tree (or acyclic graph) via DFS/BFS.  
   - lca(u, v, dist, parent): an LCA routine by depth-equalization and single-step parent jumps.  
   - Path-to-root bitmask construction: walk u and v up to their LCA, OR’ing bits corresponding to visited nodes or edges, for quick union of multiple paths via integer masks.

Simulate repeatedly reducing a binary‐represented integer to 1 by either adding one when it’s odd or dividing by two when it’s even, counting the steps needed.

A straightforward greedy simulation on a bit‐string: if the least significant bit is 1 (odd), perform a binary increment; otherwise pop the last bit (divide by two). This repeats until only one bit remains.

3. Reusable components

- Greedy simulation loop: a pattern that applies different operations based on current parity and counts steps until a termination condition.

Precompute a table of interval‐based values so that for any query interval one can instantly retrieve the maximum of some associative‐combining measure over all subintervals.

Dynamic programming over all subarrays (interval DP), with two passes:  
- First pass computes the raw associative measure (here XOR) for every subarray of each possible length in O(n²).  
- Second pass computes the maximum over all “children” intervals to allow constant‐time range‐maximum‐of‐measure queries.

3. Reusable components  
- 2D DP table construction for all subarrays: dp[len][start] = combine(dp[len–1][start], dp[len–1][start+1]).  
- In‐place propagation of range maxima: dp[len][start] = max(dp[len][start], dp[len–1][start], dp[len–1][start+1]).  
- O(1) interval query using precomputed dp[d][l] for an interval length d starting at l.
